headings.text: Example: centripetal acceleration acting on the Moon

html:
The big picture

A point moving on a circle of radius R needs only one number to say where it is: the displacement angle \varphi, measured from the x-axis, counter-clockwise positive. Angles are measured in radians: arc length divided by radius, so a full turn is 2\pi and 1\,\mathrm{rad} = 1. Rotational kinematics describes the motion through \varphi(t), with its own angular velocity \omega = \dot\varphi and angular acceleration \alpha = \dot\omega; for constant \alpha the formulas are copies of the linear ones (s \leftrightarrow \varphi, v \leftrightarrow \omega, a \leftrightarrow \alpha). In uniform circular motion (\omega constant), differentiating \vec s = R\,(\cos\omega t, \sin\omega t)^\top twice gives a constant speed R\omega along the tangent and an acceleration of size R\omega^2 = v^2/R pointing to the centre: the centripetal acceleration. The outward "centrifugal acceleration" is a pseudo acceleration. One turn takes the period T = 2\pi/\omega; the turns per second are the frequency f = 1/T. If the speed also changes, a tangential acceleration adds to the radial one.

1 Angular position

Lecture: the lecture handout p. 7–8 · Giancoli §10-1

A wheel, a robot joint or a disc turns about a fixed axis; every point of it moves on a circle around that axis. To describe the turning, follow one point P at the distance R from the axis.

The board's labels: \varphi … DISPLACEMENT ANGLE; R … RADIUS; CoR … Center of ROTATION. The position of P:

\vec s(t) = \begin{pmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} R\cdot\cos(\varphi) \\ R\cdot\sin(\varphi) \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \lvert\vec s(t)\rvert = R
Symbols
  • \vec s(t) — position of P relative to the centre of rotation (m)
  • R — radius, the constant distance from the centre (m)
  • \varphi — displacement angle from the positive x-axis to the position vector (rad)

Drop a perpendicular from P to the x-axis: a right triangle with the hypotenuse R, the angle \varphi at the centre and the legs x, y. So \cos\varphi = x/R and \sin\varphi = y/R, which gives the column (in the other quadrants \cos or \sin become negative, and so do x or y). And \lvert\vec s\rvert = \sqrt{R^2(\cos^2\varphi + \sin^2\varphi)} = R by \cos^2\varphi + \sin^2\varphi = 1. That is what "moving on a circle" means: the distance from the centre never changes, so one number, \varphi, says where the point is: the angular position. For a rigid body all its points turn through the same angle, so \varphi describes the whole body. To make \varphi a number one can compute with, it is measured in radians (section 2).

Sign of the angle. Sketch (p. 7–8): an angle drawn clockwise below the x-axis, marked "→ NEGATIVE"; one drawn counter-clockwise up to P, "\varphi … positive". "CCW, 'COUNTER CLOCK WISE', IS POSITIVE." This is the maths convention (the unit circle runs counter-clockwise), and it matches the right-hand rule from 2 Vectors and Vector Products: with x right and y up, z points out of the page, and a counter-clockwise turn is a positive turn about +z. The same sign applies to \omega and \alpha below.

Angular displacement. When the point moves from P_1 (angle \varphi_1) to P_2 (angle \varphi_2), it has turned through \Delta\varphi = \varphi_2 - \varphi_1, positive for a counter-clockwise turn. This is the rotational counterpart of the displacement \Delta x in 4 Kinematics – Position, Velocity and Acceleration.

2 Measuring angles: what's a radian

Lecture: the lecture handout p. 8–9 · Giancoli §10-1

Computing with \varphi needs an angle unit in which the arc length on a circle is simply angle × radius. The board builds it from the circumference.

Sketch: a circle with radius R.

U = R\cdot 2\cdot\pi \quad\to\quad f(\varphi)

R = 1: \quad U = 2\pi\cdot R \ \to\ \text{angle } 360^\circ, with "↑ RADIANS" under the 2\pi.

U_\frown = \pi\cdot R, \qquad U_\frown = \varphi \ldots \text{in rad} \cdot R
Symbols
  • U — circumference of the circle (m) (German Umfang)
  • U_\frown — length of the arc that belongs to the angle \varphi (m)
  • R — radius (m); \varphi — the angle at the centre, in radians

Line by line: the whole circumference belongs to the full angle, and the question is how the arc length depends on the angle, U_\frown = f(\varphi). On a circle of radius 1 the circumference is 2\pi, and the full angle 360^\circ is called 2\pi\,\mathrm{rad}. Half the circle gives the arc \pi R and the angle 180^\circ = \pi\,\mathrm{rad}. In general the arc is the same fraction of the circumference as the angle is of the full turn:

\frac{U_\frown}{2\pi R} = \frac{\varphi_\text{deg}}{360^\circ} \quad\Rightarrow\quad U_\frown = R \cdot \underbrace{\varphi_\text{deg}\cdot\frac{2\pi}{360^\circ}}_{\varphi \text{ in rad}} = \varphi\,R
Symbols
  • \varphi_\text{deg} — the angle in degrees; the bracket is the same angle in radians; other symbols as above

Sketch (p. 9): a circular sector with two radii R and the angle \varphi between them. The board's result:

U_\frown = \varphi\cdot R

Symbols as above. The radian is chosen so that no conversion factor appears: arc = angle × radius, exactly when the angle is in radians. Turned round, \varphi = U_\frown / R is a length divided by a length, so the unit cancels: [\varphi] = \mathrm{rad} is dimensionless, 1\,\mathrm{rad} = 1 (board). One radian is the angle whose arc is one radius long, 180^\circ/\pi \approx 57.3^\circ.

2\pi \mathrel{\hat=} 360^\circ, \qquad \pi \mathrel{\hat=} 180^\circ, \qquad \frac{\pi}{2} \mathrel{\hat=} 90^\circ, \qquad \frac{\pi}{4} \mathrel{\hat=} 45^\circ, \ \ldots
Symbols
  • \hat= — "corresponds to": the same angle in radians (left) and degrees (right)

30^\circ → radians (board): "\text{ANGLE}^\circ\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \ldots\ \mathrm{rad}". Since \pi\,\mathrm{rad} \mathrel{\hat=} 180^\circ, one degree is \frac{\pi}{180}\,\mathrm{rad}. The "\ldots" filled in:

30^\circ\cdot\frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{\pi}{6}\,\mathrm{rad} \approx 0.524\,\mathrm{rad}

Symbols as above. The degree signs cancel. Back the other way: multiply by \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}. On a circle of radius 2\,\mathrm m this angle cuts out an arc of \frac{\pi}{6}\cdot 2\,\mathrm m \approx 1.05\,\mathrm m.

Common mistake — degrees in a radian formula

U_\frown = \varphi R (and below v = \omega R) only holds with \varphi in radians. Inserting 30 for 30^\circ gives an arc of 30R, almost five full circumferences. Convert first, and set the calculator to RAD when evaluating \sin(\omega t) with \omega in rad/s.

3 Angular velocity and angular acceleration

Lecture: the lecture handout p. 8 · Giancoli §10-1 to §10-3

For straight motion, velocity was the derivative of the position. The board asks the same here: "\vec v = \dfrac{\mathrm d\vec s}{\mathrm dt} \ \to\ \varphi \to \varphi(t) ?". On the circle the position is fixed by the angle, so let the angle depend on time. As for straight motion, the average rate over a time \Delta t is \bar\omega = \Delta\varphi/\Delta t; letting \Delta t \to 0 gives the instantaneous rate, the derivative:

\omega(t) = \frac{\mathrm d\varphi}{\mathrm dt} = \dot\varphi, \qquad \alpha(t) = \frac{\mathrm d\omega}{\mathrm dt} = \dot\omega = \ddot\varphi
Symbols
  • \omega — angular velocity: how fast the angle grows (rad/s), Greek "omega"
  • \alpha — angular acceleration: how fast \omega changes (rad/s²), Greek "alpha"
  • counter-clockwise counts positive for both

The board names these ("ANGULAR VELOCITY", "ANGULAR ACCELERATION") without writing the definitions. It is exactly the chain s \to v \to a of 4 Kinematics – Position, Velocity and Acceleration, "rotated". All points of a rigid body share the same \omega and \alpha at any instant; what differs from point to point is the speed along the circle, v = R\omega, which grows with the radius (sections 4 and 6).

Beyond the lecture (Giancoli §10-2)

The book also treats \omega and \alpha as vectors along the axis of rotation: curl the fingers of the right hand in the direction of turning, and the thumb gives the direction of \vec\omega. A counter-clockwise turn in the x–y plane then has \vec\omega along +z, which is the lecture's "CCW positive" convention in vector form. The tutorial sketch of the CD (Problem 25, Tutorial 1 – Projectile and Circular Motion (6 Nov)) draws \vec\omega and \vec\alpha this way.

Constant angular acceleration (Giancoli §10-3). For a constant angular acceleration the board writes:

\alpha(t) = \alpha_0 = \alpha, \qquad \omega(t) = \alpha\cdot t + \omega_0, \qquad \varphi(t) = \alpha\cdot\frac{t^2}{2} + \omega_0\cdot t + \varphi_0, \qquad \alpha = \text{const.}
Symbols
  • \varphi(t) — angle at time t (rad); \varphi_0 = \varphi(t = 0\,\mathrm s) — starting angle (rad)
  • \omega(t) — angular velocity (rad/s); \omega_0 = \omega(t = 0\,\mathrm s)
  • \alpha — angular acceleration (rad/s²), here constant; t — time (s)

They come from the same two integrations as x(t) in 5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion and Free Fall:

\begin{aligned} \omega(t) &= \omega_0 + \int_0^t \alpha\,\mathrm d\tau = \omega_0 + \alpha\,t && \text{(}\alpha = \dot\omega \text{ integrated; } \alpha \text{ constant)} \\ \varphi(t) &= \varphi_0 + \int_0^t (\omega_0 + \alpha\,\tau)\,\mathrm d\tau = \varphi_0 + \omega_0\,t + \alpha\,\frac{t^2}{2} && \text{(}\omega = \dot\varphi \text{ integrated; power rule)} \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • \tau — integration variable (s); others as above

The derivation used only "\dot\omega = \alpha = \text{const}" and "\dot\varphi = \omega", never what the symbols mean, so every constant-acceleration tool carries over, including the time-free one, \omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\,(\varphi - \varphi_0). The board's LOOK-UP TABLE:

LINROT
s\varphi
v\omega
a\alpha

with the units [\varphi] = \mathrm{rad} … dimensionless, 1\,\mathrm{rad} = 1; [\omega] = \mathrm{rad/s}; [\alpha] = \mathrm{rad/s^2}; and "… ° → degree, UNIT: full circle 360^\circ". To use it, take any linear constant-acceleration formula and swap the symbols row by row: v = v_0 + at becomes \omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t.

Common mistake — the two meanings of \alpha

On this board \alpha is the launch angle in projectile motion (6 Projectile Motion) and, a page later, the angular acceleration. They have nothing to do with each other: one is an angle, the other a rate (rad/s²). In a problem that has both, rename one.

Worked example — a motor spinning up

A robot's drive motor starts from rest (\omega_0 = 0, \varphi_0 = 0) with the constant angular acceleration \alpha = 4\,\mathrm{rad/s^2}. Find \omega and the angle turned after 3\,\mathrm s.

  1. Pick the linear formula and swap symbols: v = v_0 + at \to \omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t.
  2. Angular velocity: \omega(3\,\mathrm s) = 0 + 4 \cdot 3 = 12\,\mathrm{rad/s}.
  3. Angle: \varphi(3\,\mathrm s) = \tfrac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 3^2 = 18\,\mathrm{rad}.
  4. In turns: one turn is 2\pi\,\mathrm{rad}, so 18/(2\pi) \approx 2.86 revolutions.
Problem-solving steps — rotation with constant angular acceleration
  1. Fix the positive turning direction (counter-clockwise unless told otherwise) and the start t = 0.
  2. Convert every angle to rad, every rate to rad/s or rad/s² (1 turn = 2\pi\,\mathrm{rad}, 1 rpm = 2\pi/60\,\mathrm{rad/s}).
  3. List \varphi_0, \omega_0, \alpha and the unknown; pick the linear formula that lacks what you neither know nor want, and swap symbols with the table.
  4. Solve; convert back to turns or degrees only at the end.
  5. For a point at radius R: arc = \varphi R, speed = \omega R.

4 Uniform circular motion

Lecture: the lecture handout p. 9 · Giancoli §5-2

The board: \boxed{\omega = \text{const.}}, \lvert v\rvert = \text{const}. Uniform circular motion means the angle grows at a constant rate (\alpha = 0), so the point covers equal arcs in equal times and its speed is constant. The board also contrasts two ways to describe the point: x, y, z, the CARTESIAN DOMAIN, and R, \varphi, the CIRCULAR ROTATIONAL DOMAIN (polar coordinates). The next lines translate from one to the other.

From section 3 with \alpha = 0, \omega_0 = \omega and \varphi_0 = 0 (the clock starts when P is on the positive x-axis):

\varphi(t) = \omega\cdot t
\vec s = \begin{pmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} R\cdot\cos(\omega t) \\ R\cdot\sin(\omega t) \end{pmatrix}
\vec v = \frac{\mathrm d\vec s}{\mathrm dt} = \begin{pmatrix} v_x(t) \\ v_y(t) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -R\cdot\sin(\omega t)\cdot\omega \\ R\cdot\cos(\omega t)\cdot\omega \end{pmatrix}
\vec a = \frac{\mathrm d\vec v}{\mathrm dt} = \begin{pmatrix} a_x(t) \\ a_y(t) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -R\omega^2\cos(\omega t) \\ -R\cdot\omega^2\sin(\omega t) \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • \vec s — position relative to the centre (m); R — radius (m); \omega — angular velocity (rad/s); t — time (s)
  • \vec v, v_x, v_y — velocity and its components (m/s)
  • \vec a, a_x, a_y — acceleration and its components (m/s²), circled red on the board

Each component is differentiated with the chain rule: outer function \cos or \sin, inner function \omega t with inner derivative \omega; R and \omega are constants.

\begin{aligned} v_x &= R\cdot\bigl(-\sin(\omega t)\bigr)\cdot\omega, \qquad v_y = R\cdot\cos(\omega t)\cdot\omega && \text{(}\cos' = -\sin,\ \sin' = \cos\text{, times } \omega) \\ a_x &= -R\omega\cdot\cos(\omega t)\cdot\omega = -R\omega^2\cos(\omega t) && \text{(a second } \omega \text{ from the chain rule)} \\ a_y &= R\omega\cdot\bigl(-\sin(\omega t)\bigr)\cdot\omega = -R\omega^2\sin(\omega t) && \end{aligned}

Symbols as above.

The velocity: speed R\omega, along the tangent. The board writes "\lvert v\rvert = \text{const}" without computing it:

\lvert\vec v\rvert = \sqrt{R^2\omega^2\sin^2(\omega t) + R^2\omega^2\cos^2(\omega t)} = \sqrt{R^2\omega^2\bigl(\sin^2 + \cos^2\bigr)} = R\,\omega

Symbols as above. So v = R\omega: speed along the circle = radius × angular velocity (\omega in rad/s). It is the radian rule U_\frown = \varphi R divided by time. Its direction: \vec v \cdot \vec s = (-R\omega\sin)(R\cos) + (R\omega\cos)(R\sin) = 0, so the velocity is always perpendicular to the radius, i.e. tangent to the circle, as the sketch draws it.

The acceleration: size R\omega^2, towards the centre. The board's magnitude:

\lvert\vec a\rvert = \sqrt{a_x(t)^2 + a_y(t)^2} = \sqrt{R^2\omega^4\cos^2(\omega t) + R^2\omega^4\sin^2(\omega t)} = \sqrt{R^2\omega^4\bigl(\cos^2(\omega t) + \sin^2(\omega t)\bigr)} = \sqrt{R^2\omega^4}

with \cos^2(\alpha) + \sin^2(\alpha) = 1 (this \alpha is any angle, not the angular acceleration), so

\boxed{\,\lvert\vec a\rvert = R\,\omega^2\,} \quad\to\ \text{CENTRIPETAL ACCELERATION}
Symbols
  • \lvert\vec a\rvert — size of the acceleration (m/s²), the same at every point of the circle; other symbols as above

Squaring removes the minus signs and gives (\omega^2)^2 = \omega^4; the bracket is 1; \sqrt{R^2\omega^4} = R\omega^2. Where it points, the step the board leaves out: compare \vec a with \vec s component by component, a_x = -\omega^2 \cdot R\cos(\omega t) = -\omega^2 x and a_y = -\omega^2 y, so

\vec a = -\omega^2\,\vec s

Symbols as above. \vec s points from the centre out to P; the minus sign flips it, so \vec a points from P to the centre: centripetal ("centre-seeking"). It is perpendicular to \vec v, the purely orthogonal acceleration of 4 Kinematics – Position, Velocity and Acceleration: it turns the velocity without changing the speed.

The board continues: "CENTRIFUGAL ACCELERATION → PSEUDO ACCELERATION". The outward ("centre-fleeing") acceleration you feel on a merry-go-round does not exist for an observer standing on the ground. It only appears if the motion is described from the rotating platform itself, which is why it is a pseudo acceleration.

Intuition

Without the inward acceleration the point would fly off along the tangent in a straight line. The centripetal acceleration is what bends the straight path into the circle, bit by bit. Faster turning (\omega) bends harder, and quadratically: twice the \omega, four times the acceleration.

Common mistake — "the centrifugal acceleration pushes outwards"

On a merry-go-round you feel pushed outwards, so it's tempting to add an outward acceleration. Seen from the ground there is none: your body would go straight on along the tangent, and the seat has to pull you inwards with R\omega^2 to keep you on the circle. In the kinematics of this lecture there is only the centripetal acceleration.

Common mistake — constant-acceleration formulas for circular motion

In uniform circular motion the size of \vec a is constant, but its direction keeps turning. So it is not a uniformly accelerated motion, and \vec s = \vec a t^2/2 + \vec v_0 t + \vec s_0 does not apply. Use the angle: \varphi = \omega t, v = R\omega, a = R\omega^2.

Worked example — tip of a robot arm

A robot arm turns about its base joint at the constant \omega = 1.5\,\mathrm{rad/s}; the gripper is R = 0.8\,\mathrm m from the axis.

  1. Speed of the gripper: v = R\omega = 0.8 \cdot 1.5 = 1.2\,\mathrm{m/s}, tangent to the circle.
  2. Centripetal acceleration: \lvert\vec a\rvert = R\omega^2 = 0.8 \cdot 1.5^2 = 1.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}, towards the joint axis.
  3. Check with the other form (section 5): v^2/R = 1.2^2/0.8 = 1.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2} ✓.
  4. Unit check: \mathrm m \cdot (\mathrm{rad/s})^2 = \mathrm{m/s^2}, since \mathrm{rad} = 1 ✓.

5 Period and frequency

Lecture: the lecture handout p. 1 (Week 3, 20 Oct) · Giancoli §5-2

On 20 Oct the board first rewrites the centripetal acceleration in terms of the speed, now with r for the radius:

\lvert\vec a_r\rvert = r\,\omega^2 = r\cdot\frac{v_\text{tan}^2}{r^2} = \frac{v_\text{tan}^2}{r}
Symbols
  • \vec a_r — the radial (centripetal) acceleration, pointing to the centre (m/s²)
  • r — radius (m); v_\text{tan} — tangential speed, the speed along the circle (m/s)

From v_\text{tan} = r\omega, \omega = v_\text{tan}/r and \omega^2 = v_\text{tan}^2/r^2; insert and cancel one r. This form is handy when the speed, not \omega, is given (a car in a bend).

Period. The time for one full turn: one circumference at the speed v_\text{tan}, then insert v_\text{tan} = \omega r:

T = \frac{2\pi r}{v_\text{tan}} = \frac{2\pi r}{\omega\cdot r} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}, \qquad [T] = \mathrm s
Symbols
  • T — the period: time for one full turn (s)
  • 2\pi r — circumference, the distance covered in one turn (m)

The same directly in angles: one turn is 2\pi\,\mathrm{rad} at the rate \omega.

Frequency. If one turn takes T, then 1/T turns happen per second:

f = \frac1T = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}, \qquad [f] = \mathrm{Hz}
Symbols
  • f — the frequency: number of turns per second (Hz = 1/\mathrm s)

So \omega = 2\pi f. Both \omega and f count "how fast it turns" and both have the unit 1/s (since rad = 1), but f counts turns per second and \omega counts radians per second; one turn is 2\pi rad. Writing Hz for f and rad/s for \omega keeps them apart. A wheel at f = 2\,\mathrm{Hz} has T = 0.5\,\mathrm s and \omega = 4\pi \approx 12.6\,\mathrm{rad/s}.

Example: centripetal acceleration acting on the Moon

T = 27.3 days, R = 384\,000\ \mathrm{km}; next to it v_\text{tan} = R\omega, \omega = v_\text{tan}/R. Treat the Moon's orbit as uniform circular motion: its speed is one circumference per period, v_\text{tan} = 2\pi R/T, and the centripetal acceleration is v_\text{tan}^2/R:

a_r = \Bigl(\underbrace{\frac{2\pi R}{T}}_{v_\text{tan}}\Bigr)^2\cdot\frac1R = \frac{4\pi^2 R}{T^2} = \ldots = 2.72\cdot10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}
Symbols
  • a_r — the Moon's centripetal acceleration (m/s²)
  • R — radius of the Moon's orbit around the Earth (m); T — its orbital period (s)

The "\ldots", everything converted to SI first:

\begin{aligned} T &= 27.3 \cdot 24 \cdot 3600\,\mathrm s \approx 2.359 \cdot 10^{6}\,\mathrm s, \qquad R = 384\,000\,\mathrm{km} = 3.84 \cdot 10^{8}\,\mathrm m && \text{(days} \to \text{s, km} \to \text{m)} \\ a_r &= \frac{4\pi^2 \cdot 3.84 \cdot 10^{8}\,\mathrm m}{(2.359 \cdot 10^{6}\,\mathrm s)^2} = \frac{1.516 \cdot 10^{10}\,\mathrm m}{5.564 \cdot 10^{12}\,\mathrm{s^2}} \approx 2.72 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m/s^2} && \text{(insert)} \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. Then in units of g, multiplying by a factor equal to 1:

a_r = 2.72\cdot10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{g}{9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}}}_{1} = 2.78\cdot10^{-4}\,g
Symbols
  • g \approx 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2} — gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface

Why this example: 2.78 \cdot 10^{-4} \approx 1/3600, and the Moon is about 60 Earth radii away, with 60^2 = 3600. That is Newton's check: the gravity that gives g at the surface, weakened with the square of the distance, provides exactly the Moon's centripetal acceleration (10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy). The Moon moves at about 1.0\,\mathrm{km/s}, yet its acceleration is tiny.

Video link on the board: Seafile (lecture video, AAU login).

Problem-solving steps — uniform circular motion
  1. Identify the circle: its centre and radius r.
  2. Get one rate and convert the others: \omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi/T, v_\text{tan} = r\omega (everything in SI, angles in rad).
  3. Centripetal acceleration: a_r = r\omega^2 = v_\text{tan}^2/r, pointing to the centre.
  4. Check units and size; the velocity is tangent, the acceleration radial.

6 Non-uniform circular motion

Lecture: the lecture handout p. 1 · Giancoli §5-5

If the point also speeds up or slows down along the circle, the acceleration has two parts (board):

\vec a = \vec a_\text{tan} + \vec a_r
Symbols
  • \vec a_\text{tan} — tangential acceleration (m/s²), along the direction of motion; it changes the speed; zero in uniform circular motion
  • \vec a_r — radial (centripetal) acceleration (m/s²), towards the centre; it changes the direction
  • \vec a — total acceleration, the vector sum

This is the tangential/orthogonal split of 4 Kinematics – Position, Velocity and Acceleration applied to a circle. The radial part is always v_\text{tan}^2/r, with whatever speed the point has at that moment; the tangential part is r\alpha for an angular acceleration \alpha (from v_\text{tan} = r\omega, differentiated). The two parts are perpendicular, so \lvert\vec a\rvert = \sqrt{a_\text{tan}^2 + a_r^2}.

Connection

The prep course had the rotation quantities and v = \omega R (1 Kinematics › Simple rotational/circular motion of a point mass) and the forces in circular motion (2 Dynamics › Forces in circular motion). With Newton's second law (8 Newton's Laws and Forces), m R\omega^2 becomes the centripetal force. In robotics, \varphi, \omega, \alpha are the joint angle, joint speed and joint acceleration of a revolute joint.
